The median earnings surprise for the fiscal year is the median of the distribution of earnings surprises

I include these observations in my earnings sample but I exclude them from my profit and loss samples.

For profits, I conduct a temporal analysis of the frequency of small positive profit surprise conditional on positive profit surprise.
For losses, I conduct a temporal analysis of the frequency of extreme negative loss surprise conditional on negative loss surprise.
For profits, I conduct a temporal analysis of the frequency of small positive profit surprise conditional on positive profit surprise.

method.quote: The trend and the t-value pertain to the slope coefficient of the univariate regression of the column on fiscal year.

equation.quote: First, I run separate regressions of median surprise on the fiscal year representing the firm’s fiscal quarter for earnings, profits and losses.

Second, for profit observations, I regress the median frequency of small positive surprise conditional on positive surprise occurring in the fiscal year representing the firm’s fiscal quarter on the fiscal year.

Third, for loss observations, I regress the median frequency of extreme negative surprise conditional on negative surprise occurring in the fiscal year representing the firm’s fiscal quarter on the fiscal year.
The trend and the t-value pertain to the slope coefficient of the univariate regression of the column on fiscal year.

sample.quote: I obtain 176,519 quarterly observations of actual earnings and analyst forecasts spanning the 16 years, 1984–1999.
The only constraints I impose for my principal analyses are that the I/B/E/S file contains the quarterly earnings report date
at least one earnings forecast be made before that date
The averages reported in the all years row are the time-series means of the 16 annual observations.
Earnings are reported quarterly earnings numbers in a given fiscal year.
Losses are reported negative quarterly earnings numbers in the same fiscal year.
Profits are positive quarterly earnings numbers in that fiscal year.
Earnings are occasionally zero cents per share
I include these observations in my earnings sample but I exclude them from my profit and loss samples.

I define the percent of extreme loss surprises in a given fiscal year as the number of negative quarterly loss surprises in a given fiscal year of at least 25 cents in magnitude divided by the number of negative loss surprises in the fiscal year.

review_notes: Scope: Table 1 and Figure 2 report the full-sample principal temporal analyses: three annual median-surprise trends, two sign-specific zero-surprise trends, two sign-specific positive-surprise trends, and one conditional small-positive-profit and one conditional extreme-negative-loss trend. Alternative-explanation analyses in Section 5 and growth-versus-value subgroup analyses in Section 6 are excluded.
The paper reports univariate regressions of annual statistics on fiscal year, but does not identify the underlying estimator. The method remains null rather than being assumed to be OLS.

For sign-specific zero and positive surprise rates, the table reports frequencies within the profit/loss panels; the text gives the general annual rate construction but does not separately restate the panel-specific denominator.
results_review_notes: Table 1 reports the time-series average of each selected annual outcome over 16 annual observations. No additional descriptives for the retained fiscal-year predictor are reported; later alternative-explanation and subgroup analyses are outside the frozen baseline scope.

For the extreme-negative-loss outcome, the table prints a positive t-value (13.48) beside a negative trend (−2.86); this printed statistic and the text p-value are preserved, while its sign convention remains unspecified.
